---
title: "Creating Custom Adaptors"
---

# Creating Custom Adaptors

An adaptor is an iterator that holds another iterator. `map` and `filter` are adaptors. You write one when the standard set does not name the operation you are repeating.

## The concept

The struct stores the inner iterator and whatever extra state the operation needs. `next` pulls from the inner iterator, maybe more than once, and returns `Option<Item>`. Implement `Iterator` for the struct. A small method on a trait, or a plain function that returns the struct, is how callers attach it.

Do not allocate inside `next` unless the item itself must own new data.

## Recipe 40 — A simple stateless adaptor

Scale every integer by a constant. No memory between items.

```rust
struct Scale<I> {
    inner: I,
    factor: i32,
}

impl<I> Iterator for Scale<I>
where
    I: Iterator<Item = i32>,
{
    type Item = i32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        self.inner.next().map(|n| n * self.factor)
    }
}

fn scale<I>(iter: I, factor: i32) -> Scale<I>
where
    I: Iterator<Item = i32>,
{
    Scale { inner: iter, factor }
}

fn main() {
    let out: Vec<_> = scale([2, 3, 4].into_iter(), 10).collect();
    assert_eq!(out, [20, 30, 40]);
}
```

`map(|n| n * 10)` already does this. The recipe is the shape: one field for the inner iterator, one field for the parameter, `next` delegates.

## Recipe 41 — A stateful adaptor with an accumulator

Yield the running total. The accumulator is a field, because `next` only receives `&mut self`.

```rust
struct RunningTotal<I> {
    inner: I,
    total: i32,
}

impl<I> Iterator for RunningTotal<I>
where
    I: Iterator<Item = i32>,
{
    type Item = i32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let n = self.inner.next()?;
        self.total += n;
        Some(self.total)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let totals: Vec<_> = RunningTotal { inner: [10, 5, 1].into_iter(), total: 0 }.collect();
    assert_eq!(totals, [10, 15, 16]);
}
```

`scan` in the standard library is this adaptor with a closure. Reach for `scan` in application code. Write the struct when you are building a reusable type with a name.

## Recipe 42 — An adaptor that transforms and filters simultaneously

Keep positive readings and convert them to `f64` degrees. One pass, no intermediate `Vec`.

```rust
struct PositiveAsFloat<I> {
    inner: I,
}

impl<I> Iterator for PositiveAsFloat<I>
where
    I: Iterator<Item = i32>,
{
    type Item = f64;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        loop {
            match self.inner.next() {
                Some(n) if n > 0 => return Some(f64::from(n)),
                Some(_) => continue,
                None => return None,
            }
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let kept: Vec<_> = PositiveAsFloat { inner: [0, 3, -1, 8].into_iter() }.collect();
    assert_eq!(kept, [3.0, 8.0]);
}
```

The loop inside `next` is the important part. One call to `next` may pull several inner items before it has something to yield. `filter_map` is the standard-library spelling of this recipe.

## Recipe 43 — A generic adaptor with full type flexibility

Take any item type and any closure that maps `A` to `B`. This is `map`, written out.

```rust
struct MapAdapt<I, F> {
    inner: I,
    f: F,
}

impl<I, F, B> Iterator for MapAdapt<I, F>
where
    I: Iterator,
    F: FnMut(I::Item) -> B,
{
    type Item = B;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        self.inner.next().map(&mut self.f)
    }
}

fn map_adapt<I, F, B>(inner: I, f: F) -> MapAdapt<I, F>
where
    I: Iterator,
    F: FnMut(I::Item) -> B,
{
    MapAdapt { inner, f }
}

fn main() {
    let labels: Vec<String> = map_adapt(["ada", "linus"].into_iter(), |name| name.to_uppercase()).collect();
    assert_eq!(labels, ["ADA", "LINUS"]);
}
```

`F: FnMut(I::Item) -> B` is the bound. `FnMut` because `next` may call it many times and may need to mutate captured state. `FnOnce` would be consumed on the first item. `Fn` would forbid that state.

Calling `self.inner.next().map(&mut self.f)` works because `Option::map` takes a `FnOnce`, and `&mut F` implements `FnOnce` when `F: FnMut`. Writing `|item| (self.f)(item)` also works and is easier to read if the closure needs a second field from `self`.
